newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian, Chechen leaders meet to mull future.
newsitem.headline: Russian, Chechen leaders meet to mull future.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov met on Monday for difficult talks on future relations between Moscow and its breakaway province, Itar-Tass news agency said.

Tass quoted Yeltsin as saying before the talks started in the Kremlin that he hoped for "sincere" dialogue with Maskhadov. Maskhadov echoed Yeltsin's words, adding that he hoped for a positive result from the meeting.
The Kremlin talks are likely to be overshadowed by apparent disagreements between the Kremlin and the separatists over the mainly Moslem region's future.

Interfax news agency quoted Maskhadov as saying before his departure from the regional capital Grozny that he hoped to persuade Yeltsin to recognise formally Chechnya's effective independence in a full-scale political treaty.

"These relations (between Russia and Chechnya) should be equal, based on a full-scale inter-state treaty which would envisage mutual recognition, establishing embassies and non-interference in each other's internal affairs," he said.

Russian officials have made clear that they are not willing even to discuss Chechnya's claims to full independence, which they see as a breach of a peace deal signed a year ago after 20 months of war in which tens of thousands of people were killed.
Under the peace deal, Russia pulled its forces out of the rebel region and the separatist leaders agreed to delay a decision on Chechnya's future political status until 2001.
The rebel leaders say their region is independent and they view the delay simply as a breathing space for Moscow to find a face-saving way of letting Chechnya formally secede.

The Chechen first deputy premier, Movladi Udugov, said on Sunday that Grozny wanted Moscow to pay for the damage wrought by its troops during the fighting, a staggering $260 billion -- more than half Russia's entire annual national income.
Moscow views Chechnya as part of the Russian federation and hopes that in four years it will find a compromise with Grozny which would keep the region from seceding.
Russian officials have said that Yeltsin is planning to discuss with Maskhadov Moscow's economic assistance to Chechnya.

He will also urge Maskhadov to free Russians and a number of foreigners still being held in Chechnya and make efforts to clamp down on banditry, which has flourished in the southern province for years.
Udugov said on Sunday that two journalists from a private Russian television company, seized on June 11, had been freed on the eve of the talks.
Three journalists from the NTV commercial channel, seized more than three months ago, are still in captivity somewhere in Chechnya.
Two Britons, five French people, a German, a Slovak and a Yugoslav are among those currently missing in Chechnya.
Russian Security Council Secretary Ivan Rybkin, the main Kremlin negotiator with Chechnya, has said the number of people still missing, including captives taken during the war, totals 1,407.
